## III. A stronger continuum theorem: emitted radiation cannot all return at finite time

Consider a fixed radiation Hilbert space `H_rad = L^2(I,domega) tensor K`, with free Hamiltonian multiplication by `omega`, initially vacuum in the one-photon sector. Suppose finite-dimensional emitter amplitudes `q(t)` couple to the bath through

    (W q)(omega) = v(omega) R q,

where `R:C^d -> K` is time independent, and `|v(omega)|>0` almost everywhere on some nonempty open interval `I0 subset I`. The internal Hamiltonian may be arbitrary and time dependent; assume only that the total evolution is well-defined, the coupling is bounded/finite-energy, and the transfer takes finite time `T`.

The exact radiation amplitude at the end is

    psi_rad(omega,T) = -i v(omega)e^{-i omega T}
                          int_0^T e^{i omega t} R q(t) dt.       (4)

Each component of the Fourier integral in (4) is an **entire** function of complex `omega`, since `R q(t)` has support in the finite interval `[0,T]`. If the final radiation sector is *exactly vacuum* across a nonzero frequency interval, the identity theorem for holomorphic functions and uniqueness of the Fourier transform require

    R q(t) = 0  for almost every t in [0,T].                    (5)

This is stronger than the instantaneous condition for remaining radiation-vacuum at every time: **even coherent reabsorption at the final time cannot perfectly erase broadband radiation unless the emitter trajectory is in the common radiative kernel throughout.**

In particular, if `R` has full column rank, then `q(t)=0` a.e.; with no `a-b` bypass, exact finite-time `a->b` transfer and exact final radiation vacuum cannot both occur. If `ker R` is nonzero, (5) gives a necessary condition, not an automatic controllability theorem. A factorized shared-bath example below supplies sufficiency at this interface.

This theorem is about a stationary, freely propagating continuum with frequency-separable `v(omega) R`. For general nonfactorizable `W(omega)`, simultaneous spectral-kernel properties need their own analysis; in particular, on-shell scattering cancellation need not imply a time-independent dark state. A finite discrete bath is a decisive counterexample to careless generalization: a two-state emitter/radiation Rabi system returns all radiation to vacuum after `pi/g` despite fully populating that radiation mode transiently.

STATIONARY FACTORIZED RADIATION AND ESCAPES
For stationary W(omega)=v(omega)R, v nonzero on an open interval and a well-defined finite-energy coupling, final vacuum forces the finite-time Fourier transform of Rq to vanish on an interval. It is entire, hence zero, and Fourier uniqueness gives Rq(t)=0 almost everywhere. With R full column rank, no mediator history is possible; diagonal PHP then forbids transfer. A nontrivial kernel is necessary, not sufficient for controllability. A finite discrete bath can revive and is a counterexample to extending the proof beyond the open continuum interval.
The fixed-occupation history sin(pi*t/T)exp(-iM*t) has vanishing overlap with a fixed frequency band as M increases. This disproves a universal quantitative radiation floor based only on occupation. M is a growing modulation resource, and this history is not automatically a complete controlled transfer. A fixed finite-dimensional temporal space has a positive Gram minimum, which can collapse when the space grows. Its numerical quadrature is not a dimension-uniform physical floor.
A direct imaginary a-b counterdiabatic edge provides the dark path but violates the no-bypass PHP premise and pays a loop phase/control interface. A common collective radiation matrix with kernel(1,-1) allows an addressed antisymmetric emitter mode. Independent loss channels or frequency-dependent which-path columns can destroy that common kernel. These are distinct physical changes, not a generic cancellation of spontaneous radiation.
The last1515 section's dipole formulas were checked against the primary PMC8551341 article's explicit formulas immediately before Eq31 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8551341/). Its convention is gamma=Gamma/2, g=Omega12 and Gamma12=2gamma12. Under that conversion the supplied decay/exchange formulas agree. Taylor expansion gives dark decay ratios x^2/5 transverse and x^2/10 longitudinal, while exchange grows as3/(4x^3) or-3/(2x^3). These are point-dipole free-space Born–Markov/RWA estimates with a paid large near-field exchange and model-breakdown risks, not a universal device lower bound or a recovered experimental measurement. The example with Gamma/B1 does not establish the approximation's physical validity. No long third-party text is republished.
